rows.result: As hostile as the situation allows, and they move to attack or drive the party off at once.
Wary and unfriendly, weapons ready, with no patience for questions or delays.
Cautious and neutral, willing to talk while keeping one eye on the road behind them.
Well disposed and willing, glad to trade news, goods, or directions without much pressing.
Genuinely friendly and helpful, and they share what little they have as far as their means allow.
A river changed course and moved a whole district's wealth to a neighbor.
A mercenary company was dismissed without pay at the end of a campaign.
A poor harvest coincided with a tax increase and a rumor of hoarding.
A road was closed for repairs and left a trade town without customers.
A healer was accused of poisoning a noble child and fled before trial.
A border marker was moved during a single night of heavy rain.
A shipment of grain arrived spoiled and the merchants blamed each other.
A marriage contract was broken after the bride's family lost its fortune.

name: What Became of the First People

rows.result: They kept their own courts in three valleys and answer to no one else.
They were pushed into the least fertile hills and still farm there.
They were absorbed so completely that only a few words of their speech remain.
They were converted, renamed, and taught to forget their own genealogies.
They were wiped out by sickness before any treaty could be made.
They became the new rulers by marrying into the incoming houses.
No two accounts agree whether they fled, died, or were simply absorbed.
They were hired as soldiers and settled as a separate quarter in every town.
They were gone before the first settlers arrived, leaving only field boundaries.
They fled across the water and their descendants still raid the coast.
A marriage and a border adjustment bought them a decade of peace.
A merchant league lent them the money at terms that crippled them for years.
They abandoned the outer districts and held the river line instead.
The cities agreed to share grain and troops under a temporary council.
They gave up a province and a generation of pride to save the rest.
They dug canals, rebuilt bridges, and paid for it with three years of hunger.
A single leader held the factions together long enough to outlast the danger.
They made a bargain with a local power that everyone agreed never to discuss.
They let the plague burn through the outer wards and sealed the inner ones.
They borrowed heavily, traded their way out, and repaid every creditor.
The hidden mark of a mutual-aid brotherhood, given in the handshake and the password.
A debt of hospitality owed between households, renewed by gifts and remembered by both.
The guild of licensed beggars, whose members hold territory and settle disputes among themselves.
A pact with a local spirit of place, inherited with the fields and renewed at sowing.
A trade secret held by a few families who will not teach it to outsiders.
Membership in a household cult that keeps its own hearth and buries its own dead.
A shared ancestor said to have walked out of the marsh with a rope of iron.
Membership in a craft guild that sets the price of every pot and pane in the district.
Closeness to the old ruling line, reckoned through cadet branches and half-remembered cousins.
A sworn compact sealed by sharing a cup, by which unrelated households settle disputes together.
A vow of pilgrimage taken by a whole household, binding them to a shared road and shrine.
A blood-oath between two families that makes cousins of strangers and enemies of their enemies.
Membership in a herding band that moves with the seasons and claims pasture by custom.
The road one's people have always traveled, with its fairs and its scattered kin.
The trade cant one speaks, which marks a person as belonging wherever the work is done.
Descent from a single grandmother whose name every household still recites at births.
Being bound to a temple as a servant, whether or not one ever takes vows.
Membership in a freeholders' assembly that votes on commons and fences and admits by petition.
The clan one marries into, since a person keeps their birth clan only until the wedding.
The order of singers who keep the family histories and admit new members by apprenticeship.
They carry a faint smell of woodsmoke and resin that clings even after washing.
Their second and third toes are joined by a web of skin, and sandals are cut to show it.
They carry their weight high on the shoulders, with long necks and narrow hips.
They heal slowly and scar generously, so most adults wear a record of their work on their hands.
Their eyebrows meet above the nose, a trait families read as a sign of temper.
They tan very dark in summer and go pale as paper in winter, with little in between.
Nearly all have a white forelock from birth, worn long or shorn without ceremony.
Their fingers are stained a permanent brown from the dye vats, a mark no washing removes.
Their teeth are small and close-set, giving every smile a childlike look.
Their hands are long-fingered and double-jointed, and they can tell one knot from another by touch.
Most have a gap between the front teeth, and children are taught to whistle through it.
They sleep in short stretches and wake at the least sound, which strangers find unnerving.
Most people are short and broad, built low to the ground and hard to knock over.
Thick, dark calluses cover the palms from an early age and never fade.
Most have a high, narrow palate and speak through the nose, a sound their neighbors mimic.
Almost all are left-handed, and their tools and looms are built the other way around.
A faint birthmark behind the left ear is so common that it is barely remarked.
They walk with a slight forward stoop from a lifetime of carrying loads on the back.
Their faces freckle so heavily in summer that the pattern is used to tell families apart.
Most have a heavy brow and a strong jaw, which makes them seem to glower when calm.
Chalk stripes on the cheeks for mourning.
A single earring of hammered tin.
Crushed pine rubbed into the hair.
Wide felt hats with a feather at the back.
Braided hair pinned with bone pins.
A strip shaved above each ear.
Twisted iron neck-rings worn tight at the throat.
A patchwork sash marking a household.
Silver wire wound through the beard.
Copper rings on every finger but the thumb.
Linen wraps dyed with walnut stain.
Tattooed bands around the wrists.
Salt-and-pepper by thirty, waved and close-cropped.
Chestnut brown, straight and heavy as a rope.
Dull brown, coarse and dry, usually braided with grease.
Honey blond, thick and loosely curled.
Mousy brown, limp and easily oiled flat.
Thinning early, most keeping what remains cropped close.
Red-gold, coarse and stiff, worn long by everyone.
Pale flaxen, fine and prone to tangling.
Golden tan, deepening to bronze in summer.
Sallow and gray-tinged from long winters indoors.
Ruddy and weathered, permanently flushed from cold.
Very pale, burning easily and rarely seen in full sun.
Rich umber, weathered darker on hands and face.
Dark mahogany with a cool, even tone.
Copper-brown, freckled across the nose.
Olive with a golden cast, dry from wind.
Hazel, shifting from green to brown with the light.
Gray-green, with lids that fold low at the outer corner.
Warm brown, with a heavy fold above the lid.
Near-black, wide and round.
Pale blue, narrowed by a lifetime of bright snow.
Cornflower blue, wide and quick.
One brown and one green, common enough to be unremarkable.
Pale gray, almost silver in winter.
Every household keeps a hearth shrine, and respected elders lead the rites without any ordained rank.
A council of senior priests who must agree before any doctrine is taught in public.
Two rival temple heads in separate cities, each with clergy and shrines, neither willing to yield.
Congregations of ordinary believers that hire their clergy by the season and argue doctrine at every meeting.
Wandering preachers with no fixed temple, each gathering a following and moving on before it hardens.
The faith is a branch of the crown, its priests appointed and paid as officials.
No central authority at all; each region keeps its own rites under a shared name.
A society of healers who serve as clergy, treating the sick as part of every rite.
The scars left after a wound, as proof that a body survived.
The protection of children and the naming of the newborn.
The echoes in caves and the voices that answer from the dark.
Storms, and the rain that comes too late or too hard.
The turning of the seasons, and the signs that announce each one.
Hospitality, and the duty owed to a stranger at the door.
The making of marriages and the households they create.
The craft of weaving, and the thread that holds a household together.
The setting of boundaries and the stones that mark them.
The trade road and the safety of those who travel it.
The forging of metal, and the fire that makes it obedient.
Healing, and the binding of wounds in body and household.
The silence after snow, and the stillness that follows a burial.
The weight of a promise made over running water.
The brewing of beer, and the songs that make a long night pass.
The care of the dead and the safe keeping of their names.
The stars, and the patterns by which farmers and travelers time their work.
The bones of the earth, and the mines that open them.
Dreams, and the messages that arrive in sleep.
The keeping of bees and the sweetness that comes from patient work.
Believers must make a pilgrimage to a shrine at least once in their lives.
Believers must fast from all cooked food for three days after a funeral.
The faithful must give a coin to every beggar at the temple gate, without exception.
Believers must pour a cup of every drink onto the ground before tasting it.
No believer may cross running water on the day of the dead.
A believer may not swear an oath without a witness from the temple.
Every adult must learn the lineage chant of their household and recite it at festivals.
The first catch of every season must be given whole to the temple, never eaten by the catcher.
Each adult must walk the boundary of the temple's land once a year and touch every marker stone.
The faithful must bring any dispute to the temple before taking it to a lord.
No one may sit at a table where an unbroken bone has been left, lest the meal offend the dead.
The faithful must have their children blessed before the first year is out.
No believer may sell a horse, a boat, or a plow to an outsider without the temple's leave.
No believer may carry iron into a place of worship.
Believers may not eat the flesh of any animal that was not bled and blessed first.
Believers must speak the names of their dead aloud once each month.
Believers must pray at dawn facing the nearest standing stone, wherever they are.
Believers must give their second-best garment to the temple each spring.
Every household must bake a loaf on the eve of the week and give it to a stranger.
The faithful may not eat alone, and must share any meal with whoever is present.
The temple has been rebuilt so often that it is a patchwork of five architectures.
The temple is a converted granary, its grain chutes still visible in the ceiling.
A spring rises under the altar and runs out through a channel in the floor.
The temple stands on a raft of lashed timbers that rises with the flood.
The interior smells always of cedar, even when no cedar burns.
A cracked bell hangs in the courtyard and is rung only for funerals.
The interior is painted floor to ceiling in a single faded red.
The roof is a single great tree trunk, hollowed and laid across the walls.
Its tower leans so far that the whole building seems about to follow.
The temple is cut into a hillside, its entrance a plain door in a field.
Its walls are carved with a genealogical list that has run out of room.
Its facade is covered in a mosaic of broken pottery from the whole district.
Its courtyard is a maze of low walls that pilgrims must walk before entering.
The temple is built of sun-dried brick, renewed every few years by the congregation.
A hundred small clay lamps line every ledge, lit at dusk and never all at once.
Its altar is a single block of black stone said to have fallen from the sky.
A narrow stair spirals down to a pool where the faithful wash their hands.
Its walls are built from the salvaged stones of three older shrines, none matching.
A great iron hook hangs above the altar, and no one will say what it held.
Its doors are hammered bronze and show the temple's history in relief.
It grants its faithful a run of luck in trade, so long as the tithe is paid on time.
It gives its members a place in a household that will never cast them out.
It promises that the faithful will be remembered by name after death and their enemies forgotten.
It grants the faithful dreams of their enemies' plans, vivid and usually accurate.
It makes the crops of the faithful grow and the crops of their neighbors fail.
It teaches the names of small spirits, by which the faithful can command them.
It offers protection from a plague that it alone seems to foresee.
It lets parents choose the health of a child before it is born.
It forgives any crime, so long as the crime is confessed to the cult and not the law.
It shares out the property of members who die, and its members die conveniently.
It teaches a song that makes beasts and children obedient to the singer.
It lets the faithful speak with the dead, who answer truthfully if the price is paid.
It teaches that the poor carry a greater share of the world's power and the rich have stolen it.
It recruits the desperate with food, shelter, and a name.
The cult records every member's wrongdoings in writing and uses the record as leverage.
It meets in plain sight as a burial society, and members wear a common token.
It forbids members to speak of the cult to outsiders, even under torture.
It celebrates its founding with a feast that outsiders are never allowed to see.
It recruits from a single trade, and every member owes their place to another member.
It has no temple but meets wherever its leader happens to be staying.
It marks its members with a small tattoo in a place clothing covers.
It holds that the world is a dream and that acts committed in dreams are real.
It is divided into ranks, and advancement requires the betrayal of a fellow member.
It teaches that the gods are dead and that the cult's ancestors killed them.
It requires each member to keep a vigil one night a month, taking turns so the vigil never ends.
It adopts orphans and raises them as its own, and they are loyal beyond reason.
It holds its rites in the ruins of an older temple and calls them a restoration.
Its leaders are chosen by lot and serve until they die.
It keeps a rented house in every town, always under a false name.
It keeps its sacred text in memory rather than writing and recites it in a single night.
It holds that children born in a certain month belong to the cult.
Members give up their family names on joining and take new ones from a list of the dead.
A lord planted this settlement to hold a border he no longer defends, and the people stayed anyway.
A leper house was built well away from the town, and healthy families followed to sell to it.
A spring that never freezes made this the only winter stop between two market towns.
A road-warden's tower stood here once, and the village grew up servicing the men who guarded the crossing.
A fishing weir built across the narrow channel feeds the village and supplies three inland markets.
Herds winter in the shallow valley, and the herders' seasonal huts slowly became houses with chimneys.
Pilgrims walking to a shrine three hills over need one night's shelter, and this is the sheltered place.
The villagers hold an old oath binding them to keep the bridge here repaired and staffed.
Two roads meet at this ford, and the village exists to move carts across and charge them for it.
The old quarry left a shelf of flat stone, and anyone wanting a dry floor came here to build.
A seam of iron-bearing rock broke the surface, and the village grew around the first two shafts.
Salt pans along the flats give work for six weeks each summer and nothing at all the rest of the year.
A tall wooden crane stands over the millpond, its rope swinging free and its hook empty.
Every roof is weighted with the same grey stones, stacked in patterns that look deliberate.
Bright painted shutters mark the houses rebuilt after the fire, and nothing else is painted.
A timber scaffold leans against the church tower, unfinished for longer than anyone remembers.
Hedges of thorn divide the village into quarters, each with its own gap and its own gate.
The smell of boiling hides reaches you a mile off, and the tanners' sheds sit at the entrance.
Half the houses stand empty, shutters nailed shut and doorways filled with stacked firewood.
A single street of packed clay, wide enough for one cart and lined with open drains.
The lane narrows to a shoulder's width at the middle, where two houses lean together overhead.
A line of standing stones crosses the village green, and the houses are built between them.
The houses turn their backs to the road, and every door faces the fields instead.
A wall of stacked fieldstone circles the village, too low to stop a man and too high to step over.
They ask you to swear a dead man's debts were paid, and hand you his tally sticks.
The headman offers free lodging to anyone willing to sit up all night in the granary.
The village wants you to witness a sale of land and swear the buyer was sober.
They invite you to judge a contest of strength, and both champions are related to the headman.
A young woman begs passage out with your party and offers to pay in her family's silver.
The village offers a guide to the next town if you first help raise a fallen beam.
Someone has been stealing from the shrine, and the villagers want an outsider to say who.
The elders ask you to carry word to a hermit up the valley that his brother has died.
A widow insists you drink at her table before you leave, and her sons block the door politely.
They ask every traveller to carry a sealed letter to the next town and will not say what it holds.
A boy follows your party out of the village and refuses to go back, offering to work.
The villagers will not sell you food until you agree to look at a sick child.
Wine from the south must be landed and rested here before it survives the road north.
A great fair held once a year became a fair held every month, and then a permanent town.
The city grew to serve a garrison that never disbanded and slowly turned into a government.
It began as a winter camp for herders and became a market because everyone came there anyway.
The city grew behind a fortress that guarded the only pass through the mountains and taxed it.
A river wide enough for barges meets a road that carries wool, so cargo must change hands here.
The city holds the only bridge for eighty miles, and everything crossing the river pays at it.
The city stands where three roads meet at a shallow lake, and the lake supplies salt and fish.
A duke moved his court here to escape a plague in his old capital and never moved back.
A river delta gives shelter to a hundred hulls and enough mud to beach them for repairs.
A temple's relic drew pilgrims, the pilgrims drew merchants, and the merchants paid for the walls.
The old realm's capital fell, and this city inherited its clerks, its records, and its claims.
The city has no rubbish heaps: night carts collect everything and tip it into the marsh outside the wall.
The harbour stinks of fish oil and pitch, and the smell reaches the hill districts by midmorning.
The whole city smells of baking bread at dawn and of the drains two hours later.
Bells in a dozen shrines compete every noon, and the result is a sound like a collapsing barn.
A wall of black basalt runs through the city, older than any building and impossible to cut.
Lime dust hangs over the tanners' quarter, and the people who work there look grey as stones.
A bronze bell in the great tower is rung by hand each hour, and the whole city sets its day by it.
A canal cuts the city in two, and the only crossings are seven narrow footbridges with steep steps.
The river runs brown through the city and emerges clean, because the dyers are forbidden upstream.
Rows of elms line the main street, planted so evenly that the road looks longer than it is.
A wooden tower of scaffolding rises over the cathedral, and it is now older than the cathedral.
A thousand pigeons live in the temple eaves, and their cooing is the loudest sound at dawn.
A stranger must burn a coin at the temple of the gate before entering the inner city.
The watch demands a hostage for any party carrying more than two blades through the gate.
The gate scribes record your name, your business, and your face, then sell the record to anyone.
Every visitor is expected to attend the ruler's public audience and present a gift there.
The guilds set a fixed price for lodging, and any inn charging less is closed by morning.
The customs house opens your packs, values your goods, and offers to buy them at that value.
A rite at the city gate requires you to state aloud why you came, and the answer is recorded.
Any foreigner doing business must first buy a year's membership in a trade hall.
A toll is owed on every weapon longer than a forearm, payable at each district boundary.
The city requires every visitor to name a local sponsor, and sponsors charge for the honour.
You must stand surety for any local you speak to, or the watch takes your goods instead.
No one may trade inside the walls without a guild token, and tokens cost more than most visitors carry.
Their woodlands supply pitch and charcoal to the cities, and they follow the cutting.
They raise horses on open grass and sell the surplus to any army that pays in iron.
Their valleys flood every spring, so they farm the terraces and move their houses twice a year.
Their herds need salt, and their route follows the licks around the edge of the waste.
They live by wrecking and salvage on a dangerous coast, and their own boats are deliberately poor.
The band broke from a larger people over a marriage and has kept its distance ever since.
Their land was taken by a stronger band, so they raid the roads of the people who took it.
The forest gives them game, timber, and cover, and they have not left it in six generations.
They cut salt from a dry lake bed and trade it inland for grain they cannot grow.
A long drought emptied their homeland, and they have wandered since looking for water they trust.
A blood feud with the lowland towns keeps them in the hills, where they can see riders coming.
They hold a pass that everyone must use and charge for it instead of farming the thin soil.
Their horses are marked with a painted hand on the flank, and so are their prisoners.
They ride small, shaggy horses and never dismount to speak, even to their own elders.
The band travels with carts instead of pack animals, and the carts are painted with old battles.
They carry their dead with them for a season before burying, wrapped in painted cloth.
Their camp circle is marked by a ring of flat stones no one is allowed to step over.
Every adult wears a strip of dyed cloth on the left arm, and the pattern shows which family.
Their camps are ringed with the skulls of their own herd animals, set on poles facing outward.
Their faces are painted with ash and grease in a pattern that changes at each new moon.
Their camp moves with a train of dogs that howl all night and sleep all day.
Their clothes are sewn with small bells, muffled in the hunt and unstopped in war.
Their tents are made of stitched hide, and every seam is marked with a knot of human hair.
They cut their hair only when someone dies, so its length tells you what they have lost.
The band asks you to carry a challenge to a rival chief and repeat his answer word for word.
They ask you to find a boy who ran off to the towns and bring him back, willing or not.
They ask you to settle which of two brothers should lead, and will hold you to your answer.
They want a written promise from your party and have no one who can read it aloud.
They want iron, and will trade hides, horses, and safe passage for any blade you can spare.
A dying elder wants news of the world before he dies, and will pay in directions.
They ask you to stand witness that a stolen herd changed hands fairly.
They want a stranger's oath to seal a treaty, because no one among them is trusted to swear.
They want to buy your horses and will steal them if the price is refused twice.
The band wants a song about itself and will trade a guide for one that is good.
They demand you take one of their young to the next town and leave him there.
They demand a gift for crossing their ground, and refuse coin as an insult to the giver.
An old manor sunk to the windowsills in a peat bog.
A silver mine abandoned mid-shift, carts still loaded at the tunnel mouth.
A monastery with one bell tower standing and no other building whole.
A sea cave the tide fills twice a day and leaves toys in.
A hillside tomb whose lintel bears a name no living tongue can read.
A walled orchard where the trees bear fruit out of season.
A quarry cut into a cliff, its terraces carved with unfinished figures.
A ring of tiered stone seats, its floor swept and freshly raked.
A royal hunting lodge in woods that no hunter now enters.
A dry cistern the size of a cathedral, with a town built inside it.
A great hall where every sound returns doubled, in someone else's voice.
A mosaic floor showing a city that does not exist, updated with new streets.
A gallery of portraits where one face appears in every frame.
A table set for thirty, with food laid out and still warm.
A gate standing alone in a meadow, its posts set in dressed stone.
A library of clay tablets shelved in an order no one can parse.
A well in the courtyard that goes down further than the hill does.
A staircase of forty steps that arrives at the top with forty-one.
A room of clay jars, each sealed with wax and humming faintly.
A door of green bronze that opens only outward, by a mechanism no one has found.
The stairs spiral around a hole with no rail, and the treads get narrower toward the bottom.
A guardian beast sleeps under a heap of rags and wakes if anyone speaks above a whisper.
A glass floor over a deep well shows the safe path only from one side of the room.
An iron bell hangs by the door, rigged to ring when the door swings past a certain point.
Old mortar sifts from the arch in a fine dust, and the arch settles with each loud noise.
Mushrooms grow thick on the rotten floorbeams, and their spores fill the air when disturbed.
A ward of cold hangs in the arch, and it drains the warmth from anyone carrying metal through it.
The room floods slowly whenever the door is propped open, filling to shoulder height in an hour.
A wall of loose bricks is shored up by a single timber that has almost finished burning through.
Chalk marks on the wall count down the passages, and the marks are wrong past the seventh.
The air in the room is heavy and sweet, and earlier arrivals lie near the only vent.
Stair treads are cut unevenly on purpose, so anyone hurrying down them misjudges the last three.
The old furnace still holds heat and vents through a grate where someone will step.
The cistern's cover is cracked and hidden under silt, and the water below is deep and cold.
A stone door closes behind each person who enters, and the counterweight only works from outside.
A pressure plate sits in the centre of the doorway, greased so that even a careful step slides.
The mirror in the hall shows the room as it was, and the figure in it turns when you turn.
A nest of pale spiders lives in the roof beams, and they drop on anyone carrying a light.
Two corpses sit at a table with full cups, and the cups are laced for whoever drinks next.
The floor is a thin crust over a flooded cellar, and it cracks where the mortar has gone grey.
A rope ladder hangs into a shaft, and the shaft ends on a ledge six feet down.
A journal's last page warns that the east door is death, and the east door leads to a closet.
A shrine to an unknown god holds a bowl of coins that crumble when lifted.
An iron cage hangs from the ceiling with a skeleton inside, and the cage has never been locked.
A body in fine armour lies on a heap of gold that is painted wood and worth nothing.
A single candle burns in the empty hall, recently lit, and no one has been here for days.
The corpse of a rival team hangs from a beam, and the rope is newer than the corpse.
Fresh footprints cross the dust and lead straight into a wall that has no seam.
A stair winds up into darkness, and the top step is only four feet above the floor.
A nest of eggs in the corner draws the eye away from the shells already cracked by the exit.
A bell mechanism hangs above the entrance and is missing the striker that would ring it.
A brass key on a chain hangs from a peg by the door, and no lock in the place fits it.
A fine sword stands in the floor of the hall, and the blade is soft tin dressed to look keen.
A great stone face in the wall weeps water, and the water runs from a crack far above.
A pile of coins glitters under a shaft of light, and the coins are lead slugs painted gold.
The old library holds shelves of blank books, arranged with great care and dusted often.
A long corridor of doors gives onto small cells, all empty, all with their bolt on the outside.
An old map scratched into the wall marks a treasure room that the builder never finished.
Someone has chalked a warning in three languages on a door, and the door opens easily.
A chorus of voices sings behind a door, and the room beyond holds only a wind gap.
The stairwell smells of the sea, though the nearest coast is four days' ride away.
A garden grows below ground with no light, and someone has pruned it recently.
Two sets of stairs climb the same tower, and neither set arrives at the same floor.
The tower has no stairs to its top, and the window above is unbroken and too small to climb.
Every lamp in the hall was filled the day the place was sealed, and all of them are still full.
The counting room's tally sticks record payments made for eleven years after the last date carved.
The map room's shelves are empty, but the dust shows where a single scroll was taken.
The bones in the crypt are all left-handed, and every one of them is a grown adult.
Someone has been sweeping the dust into neat piles, and the piles are arranged as a map.
Water runs uphill in a channel cut by hand, and no wheel or pump is anywhere in the works.
A feast was laid and abandoned mid-meal, and the bread is still soft after forty years.
A portrait has been repainted so often that the face beneath is now the size of a fist.
The place was built for a hundred people, and every bed has been slept in by two.
The dead in the courtyard fell facing the same direction, and the gate is behind them.
The same man appears in three carvings separated by two hundred years of wear.
Two graves lie outside the wall, marked with the same name and the same day.
Every room in the place is numbered, and the numbers skip from eleven to thirteen twice.
The cellar holds wine that has never been opened, and the crates are stencilled with a foreign hand.
The shrine's god has two faces, and the prayers carved beneath address a third.
The guardroom's rota lists a watch of twelve, and there are only eleven bunks.
Beneath the third flagstone of the nave, in a lead box that has been soldered shut.
Inside a hollow pillar that must be broken, and the pillar holds up the only safe ceiling.
Behind the statue's base, in a cavity that opens only when the statue is turned fully round.
Under the roots of the courtyard tree, which something has been digging around at night.
In the walled-off kitchen chimney, above a fire pit that still smells strongly of smoke.
In the chimney's flue above the kitchen, wedged where only a thin arm can reach it.
Sealed inside a jar among ninety ordinary jars, and the seal is marked with a fish.
Behind the chapel's east window, in a recess reachable only from the roof by rope.
Within the guardian's harness, which must be cut free while the guardian is still upright.
In the cistern's overflow pipe, wedged tight and requiring the water to be shut off first.
In a locked ossuary rack, behind a human skull that is heavier than a skull should be.
Buried in the ash heap of the old furnace, where the heat still cracks the skin of diggers.
In the cold spring that feeds the baths, held down by a stone that must be lifted blind.
Behind the tapestry, in a niche whose covering stone is held by a rusted iron pin.
In the abbot's cell, packed inside a wax candle that has been burned down to a stub.
Under the millpond, in a millstone's central hole, hidden by silt and one deep breath.
Stitched into a corpse's coat at the bottom of the flooded shaft, under cold black water.
In the drowned archives, inside a stone book box that must be carried through waist-deep water.
In a lead coffin in the crypt, which is nailed shut and heavier than the men who nailed it.
On the highest gallery, in a bird's nest built of stolen cloth and a dead man's hair.
A tomb-city cut in tiers, where each level was sealed by a different dead house and never reopened.
An undercroft of a fallen sorcerer-realm, its halls collapsed in places and its wards still holding the rest.
A deep mine following a vein that ran out centuries ago, with the deeper galleries walled shut from inside.
A collapsed palace whose cellars go deeper than the palace stood tall, against every sensible reckoning.
A cistern-city where the reservoirs were built as halls, and the water was drawn down to hide something.
A flooded quarry whose drowned galleries were cut by masons who left their tools on the benches.
All the ruins face the same way, their doors and windows turned from the sunrise.
Every ruin here has a dry well at its centre, and each well is deeper than the hill above it.
Every doorway in these ruins is too low for a standing adult, whatever the height of the hall beyond.
Birds avoid these ruins; the ones that nest there sing a note no other bird makes.
The stones of these ruins are warm to the touch at dusk, however cold the night has turned.
Every ruin here is built of one pale stone, quarried somewhere no living mason has ever found.
A gang of children is running a rope through the flooded galleries to recover coins dropped by earlier visitors.
A surveyor with a lantern and a length of knotted cord is mapping the halls for a buyer in the capital.
Three escaped prisoners are hiding in a dry cistern and will trade what they know for a share of water.
A pair of thieves is arguing over a locked coffer they carried out but cannot open without waking something.
A band of relic pedlars is sorting grave goods by weight, arguing over which pieces carry a curse.
A grieving widow has paid a dozen mercenaries to bring back her husband's body, or what is left of it.
A chain gang and their overseer are quarrying dressed stone from the ruin itself for a new church.
A mad hermit is ringing a cracked handbell and insists the ruin has begun to count the living.
A pilgrim is kneeling at a wall of names and will not move until someone answers a question scratched there.
A physician and her apprentice are harvesting a grey fungus from the walls, filling jars with great care.
A young scholar is copying inscriptions by rushlight while her two guards play dice and ignore the dark.
Two rival heirs and their servants are cataloguing a vault's contents, each writing a different inventory.
Fifty bats hang in a dead-end vault and will not leave while a light burns beneath them.
Something with too many joints is feeding in the dark and stops whenever the party stops.
A wounded bear has taken shelter in a dry room and cannot leave without passing the party.
A rat-thing stands upright, wearing a child's shoe on one paw and holding another in its mouth.
A thing that was once a horse circles the room on too many legs and stops when it is spoken to.
A mother wolf has denned in an old shrine and her cubs are old enough to be curious about strangers.
A thin grey creature mimics the party's voices from a side passage, always one word behind.
A nest of thumb-length burrowing things lives in the dust and wakes when the floor is scuffed.
A huge pale worm comes up through the floor where warm blood has been spilled, sensing the hurt.
A bloated, dripping thing blocks the stair and slowly extends a tendril toward the nearest torch.
A blind, hairless mole-thing the size of a pony follows the party by the sound of their breathing.
A pale spider the size of a hand is spinning a web across a doorway faster than a man could walk.
A colony of the sleepless, who cannot close their eyes, keeps a lamp burning and asks the party to take a watch.
A people who bind their eyes with wax in daylight and read the walls by touch, offering to guide.
A people who speak only while touching stone will trade a secret of the ruin for a piece of iron.
A knot of pale children who speak in chorus will trade directions for one of the party's shadows.
A silent folk with painted throats hold converse by drumming on the stone with horn mallets.
A band of salt-skinned divers, who can stay dry only an hour before their skin begins to split.
A people whose joints are bound in copper wire move stiffly and ask whether the party came to wake the house.
A thin folk who drink from stone bowls have no names for themselves, only for the rooms they keep.
The mask-wearers keep a dead house's rites and will not let anyone pass a shrine with a bare face.
Two feathered people, taller than a man, are arguing over a boundary stone that moved in the night.
A thin, pale folk who live in the walls and come out to trade bone for salt and clean water.
Three gaunt figures with reed-strip skin, taller than the doors, speak a tongue that sounds like a tally.
Four workers hauling a loaded sledge through a narrow door, so nobody has a hand free for a weapon.
Two scouts crouched at a junction, drawing in the dust, one of them holding a finger to their lips.
Two groups facing each other across a hall, shouting, and neither has noticed the party yet.
A dozen figures asleep in a ring around a banked fire, with one wakeful and facing away.
Six figures eating around a table, weapons stacked in the corner, and a dog already growling.
A group hauling a closed chest up a stair, arguing about whether it has begun to move.
The trail crosses a stretch of ground where every stone is turned over, as if something searched it.
The sun sets in the wrong quarter, and every shadow the party casts agrees with it until dark.
A dead ox lies across the track, its hide unmarked, and the flies have not found it.
The party's packs are lighter by one sack when they wake, and the ground around camp is undisturbed.
The party's water tastes of iron, and every animal they pass refuses to drink from the same stream.
A sudden hailstorm strips the leaves, and the party must choose between shelter and the dry streambed.
The path runs through a stand of trees all scarred at the same height by old axe cuts.
Every bird in the valley goes silent at once, then a single bell rings from somewhere under the hill.
A flock of crows lifts from one tree at a time, moving ahead of the party as if escorting them.
A bridge over a swollen river has lost its middle third, and someone left a rope tied to the far post.
A wounded deer hobbles across the track and lies down a short way off, as if asking to be followed.
A horn sounds three times from the trees, and no one in the party can tell how far away it is.
A dog with a broken tether follows the party for a mile and then refuses to go further.
An old boundary stone has been dug up and set down facing the wrong way, with fresh mud on it.
A trader's cart stands abandoned with its goods intact and a fresh grave dug beside the wheel.
A woman on the road ahead is driving three goats and walking backwards, watching where she came from.
A man sits at a crossroads with a ledger, offering to record the party's names for a small fee.
A line of smoke rises from beyond a ridge, too thin for a camp and too steady for a fire.
A mist rises at dusk and carries the sound of a market that should be a day's ride away.
A rain-swollen stream has cut a new channel through a graveyard and is carrying bones downstream.
The floor ahead is clean and swept, in a corridor where everything else is thick with dust.
A cold draft carries the smell of wet earth and old smoke, and it is coming from a wall.
The party's shadows lengthen toward the light rather than away from it, and only for a moment.
Somewhere below, a bell rings once and the dust on every ledge shivers off.
A shadow crosses the torchlight in a closed room, and it is not cast by anyone present.
A carving of a sealed door now shows it standing open, and a narrow gap has opened beneath the image.
A slow grinding begins under the floor and the passage behind the party is shorter than it was.
A bell rope hangs in a shaft and is moving, though the shaft is too narrow for a hand.
The air changes and the torch flames bend toward a wall with no crack in it.
Water begins to seep from a seam in the ceiling, first a trickle and then a steady pour.
The last door the party forced has closed itself, and the marks of their crowbar are gone.
Two passages that were dark are now faintly lit, and the light comes from something burning.
A stone in the floor gives slightly underfoot and settles, and something below takes a breath.
A low tide sound runs through the ruin, though the party is far above any water they know of.
A door the party passed an hour ago is standing open now, though nobody touched it.
A voice recites a list of names in the next room and stops at the sound of the party's boots.
A long low sound moves through the stone, and a hairline crack opens along one wall.
Frost spreads across a wall from a single point, forming the rough shape of a doorway.
The party's echoes come back wrong, answering a beat late or in more voices than they have.
The carved faces on a wall have all turned toward the party, though the stone is unbroken.
A serpent body ending in a cluster of small arms.
A human frame wrapped in layered hide plates.
A low, broad beast that moves on six legs.
A quadruped with a human face and no eyes.
A bloated, floating sac trailing fine threads.
A tall, thin giant with limbs too long for its body.
A writhing mass of pale, rootlike tendrils.
A pillar of woven reeds and bone that walks.
A horned quadruped with a flattened, toadlike face.
A tall, gaunt humanoid with too many joints.
A pale, hairless biped that walks on its knuckles.
A many-eyed head on a spidery walking body.
To avenge a death it cannot name.
An urge no living thing can explain.
To complete a rite it was made for.
To find a mate that no longer exists.
To gather and guard bright metal.
To survive at any cost.
To be worshipped by something weaker.
To seed new broods in living hosts.
To see what happens when things break.
To return to a place that no longer exists.
To keep its young fed and hidden.
To drink from a particular spring.
It collects small objects and trades them for food.
It speaks only in questions and answers them itself.
It can only move toward what it can smell.
It is dying of something and knows it.
It remembers every face it has seen and greets them by name.
It repeats the last action it saw performed, exactly.
It will not enter a place it has not been invited.
It is terrified of its own reflection.
It casts no shadow and grows agitated in bright sun.
It counts everything it sees and becomes furious at errors.
It prefers the company of animals to people.
It follows orders given by anyone wearing a crown.
It can step through shadows but not into light.
It offers a bargain before it attacks.
It sleeps in the shape of a stone and wakes when struck.
It will stop fighting to rescue a fallen companion.
It gives away its treasure to anyone who asks politely.
It heals quickly from any wound it did not see coming.
It cannot tell the living from the dead.
It imitates the wounded cries of animals to draw people out.
